title: Examining Faculty and Student Perceptions of Generative AI in University Courses
extended_summary:
This paper examines how students and faculty perceive generative AI tools such as ChatGPT in higher education, with particular attention to perceived ease of use, ethical concerns, intentions to use, and views about impacts on learning. The study addresses a gap in empirical evidence about how attitudes toward generative AI differ across university roles and across student subgroups defined by gender and STEM versus non-STEM disciplines.

The study used an anonymous online survey grounded in a modified UTAUT framework and supplemented with items about perceived effects on learning competencies and ethics. The survey measured constructs such as performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, hedonic motivation, habit, personal innovativeness, and behavioral intention, along with views about academic integrity, policy needs, and the frequency of generative AI use. The approach was descriptive and comparative rather than experimental.

Participants were 982 students and 76 faculty members at a single large land-grant public university in the southeastern United States during the Fall 2023 semester. The student sample included both undergraduate and other university students, and analyses compared students with faculty as well as four student subgroups: STEM male, STEM female, non-STEM male, and non-STEM female. Data were collected between December 2023 and January 2024 through voluntary online survey distribution.

The authors conclude that students and faculty were broadly similar in their attitudes toward generative AI, though students reported higher ease of use, hedonic motivation, and personal innovativeness, while faculty reported more habitual use. Both groups used generative AI at similarly low rates overall and shared concerns about negative effects on learning competencies and academic dishonesty, while also supporting the development of institutional policies. Within the student sample, male STEM students tended to express the most positive attitudes and non-STEM female students the least positive, suggesting that gender and disciplinary context shape how generative AI is received in higher education.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI tools used in education broadly, including text-generating systems such as ChatGPT, considered as a general class rather than evaluated as a single product.
identified_tools.use_case: Surveyed higher-education students and faculty about perceptions, ethics, intended use, and self-reported frequency of using generative AI tools for coursework and teaching.

findings.finding_summary: In a survey of 982 students and 76 faculty at one large U.S. public university, students and faculty did not differ significantly on most attitudes toward generative AI, but students rated generative AI as easier to use (Effort Expectancy; p<0.01), more fun to use (Hedonic Motivation; p<0.05), and reported higher Personal Innovativeness (p<0.01), while faculty reported higher Habit (p<0.05). There was no significant difference in Behavioral Intention between students and faculty.
findings.measure: UTAUT-related attitude factor scores: Performance Expectancy, Effort Expectancy, Social Influence, Hedonic Motivation, Habit, Personal Innovativeness, Behavioral Intention

findings.finding_summary: Students and faculty largely agreed that generative AI would have more negative than positive effects on most learning-related competencies, including problem solving, teamwork, self-efficacy, test anxiety, intrinsic motivation, and engagement. The only significant student-faculty difference was for Academic Performance, where students were more positive than faculty (W=39,673, p<0.001).
findings.measure: Perceived impacts on critical thinking, problem-solving, teamwork, self-efficacy, test anxiety, intrinsic motivation, engagement, academic performance, and overall learning

findings.finding_summary: Students and faculty showed similar views on ethics and policy overall: both groups agreed generative AI can promote academic dishonesty, and about 80% agreed the university should develop formal policies. However, students were significantly more likely than faculty to view using generative AI for coursework as unethical (W=34,934, p=0.025) and inappropriate (W=35,334, p=0.015).
findings.measure: Ethics and policy survey items on dishonesty, appropriateness, ethicality, prohibition, and need for formal university policies

findings.finding_summary: Students and faculty reported similar frequencies of generative AI use for coursework and teaching preparation (W=33,630, p=0.542). Approximately 70% of both groups used generative AI less than once per week, with only 6% of students and 9% of faculty reporting daily use in Fall 2023.
findings.measure: Self-reported frequency of generative AI use in coursework/teaching

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical cross-sectional survey study of perceptions and self-reported use, not an intervention study evaluating causal effects on learning outcomes. The methodology is clear and sample sizes are reported, but evidence is correlational and perception-based.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report intervention effect sizes on student achievement; findings are mainly mixed perceptions, ethics concerns, and low usage rates. Reported differences are statistically significant in places but practical impact on learning is unclear.
